title: Study notes: English I
content:
Overview: building the English foundation for university study.

Key topics:
1. Grammar review: present simple vs continuous, past simple vs present perfect, future forms, articles (a/an/the), countable and uncountable nouns.
2. Sentence structure: subject–verb agreement, word order, simple, compound and complex sentences, connectors (and, but, because, although).
3. Reading skills: skimming for the main idea, scanning for details, guessing meaning from context.
4. Vocabulary: academic word families (analyse, analysis, analytical), collocations, prefixes and suffixes.
5. Writing: paragraph structure (topic sentence, supporting sentences, concluding sentence), punctuation.
6. Listening and speaking: introductions, asking questions, short presentations.

Common mistake: 'He go to university' → 'He goes to university' (third-person -s).

Practice tasks:
- Write a 120-word paragraph about your favourite course with a clear topic sentence.
- Correct: 'I am studying engineering since two years.' (→ I have been studying engineering for two years.)
- Skim a short article and state its main idea in one sentence.

title: Study notes: English II
content:
Overview: developing academic reading and writing.

Key topics:
1. Grammar: passive voice (The data was collected...), relative clauses (which, who, that), conditionals (zero, first, second), modal verbs for advice and possibility.
2. Academic reading: identifying the thesis, distinguishing facts and opinions, note-taking, summarizing.
3. Essay writing: introduction with thesis statement, body paragraphs with evidence, conclusion; essay types (descriptive, cause–effect, compare–contrast, argumentative).
4. Paraphrasing and avoiding plagiarism.
5. Academic vocabulary and formal register (avoid contractions and slang).
6. Presentations: structure, signposting phrases (First, Moving on to, To sum up).

Example paraphrase: 'Regular exercise improves concentration' → 'Students who exercise regularly tend to focus better.'

Practice tasks:
- Write a 250-word cause–effect essay on why students drop courses.
- Rewrite three active sentences in the passive.
- Summarize a one-page article in 60 words.

title: Study notes: English III
content:
Overview: advanced academic and professional English.

Key topics:
1. Advanced grammar: mixed conditionals, reported speech, nominalization (analyse → the analysis of), hedging (may, suggests, appears to).
2. Research writing: structure of a research paper (abstract, introduction, method, results, discussion), literature review, citation styles (APA, IEEE).
3. Critical reading of academic texts and evaluating sources.
4. Professional writing: emails, CVs, cover letters, reports.
5. Presentation and discussion skills: defending opinions, handling questions.
6. Interview English.

Example hedging: 'This proves the method is best' → 'These results suggest that the method may outperform the alternatives.'

Practice tasks:
- Write an abstract (150 words) for your graduation project.
- Write a formal email requesting a meeting with a professor.
- Cite a journal article in IEEE style.

title: Study notes: Technical English
content:
Overview: English for engineering and computing contexts.

Key topics:
1. Technical vocabulary: components, processes, measurements, units, abbreviations.
2. Describing things: shape, dimensions, function ('The sensor is used to measure...'), materials.
3. Describing processes and instructions: sequence words, imperatives, passive voice.
4. Reading technical documents: datasheets, manuals, specifications, standards.
5. Writing technical documents: reports, lab reports, user manuals, specifications.
6. Describing graphs and data: trends (rise, fall, peak, level off), comparisons.
7. Technical presentations.

Example: 'The graph shows that CPU temperature rose sharply from 40 °C to 85 °C within two minutes and then levelled off.'

Practice tasks:
- Write step-by-step instructions to install a program.
- Describe a line graph in 80 words.
- Read a component datasheet and list its key specifications.

title: Study notes: Writing and Presentation Skills
content:
Overview: communicating ideas clearly in writing and in front of an audience.

Key topics:
1. Planning writing: audience, purpose, outline.
2. Clear writing: short sentences, active voice, one idea per paragraph, removing filler.
3. Report writing: title, summary, introduction, body with headings, conclusions, recommendations, references.
4. Editing and proofreading checklist.
5. Presentation structure: opening hook, three main points, conclusion and call to action.
6. Slide design: one message per slide, minimal text, readable fonts, clear charts.
7. Delivery: voice, pace, eye contact, body language, managing nerves, handling questions.

Tip: the 10/20/30 guideline: about 10 slides, 20 minutes, no font smaller than 30 points.

Practice tasks:
- Rewrite a long paragraph into three clear sentences.
- Prepare a 5-minute presentation on your project with 6 slides.
- Write the executive summary of a technical report.

title: Study notes: Communication and Negotiation Skills
content:
Overview: interpersonal skills for work and teams.

Key topics:
1. Communication process: sender, message, channel, receiver, feedback, noise.
2. Verbal and non-verbal communication; active listening (paraphrase, ask, summarize).
3. Communication styles: passive, aggressive, assertive.
4. Team communication, meetings and conflict management (Thomas–Kilmann modes: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating).
5. Negotiation: positions vs interests, BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement), ZOPA, win–win (principled negotiation).
6. Persuasion and influence.
7. Professional communication: emails, phone, cross-cultural awareness.

Example: in a salary negotiation, a strong BATNA (another job offer) gives you a better position.

Practice tasks:
- Role-play a team conflict and resolve it collaboratively.
- Identify the interests behind two opposing positions.
- Rewrite an aggressive email in an assertive tone.

title: Study notes: Critical and Creative Thinking
content:
Overview: thinking clearly about arguments and generating new ideas.

Critical thinking:
1. Arguments: claims, premises, conclusions; deductive vs inductive reasoning.
2. Evaluating evidence and sources: credibility, bias, sample size.
3. Common fallacies: ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, slippery slope, hasty generalization, appeal to authority.

Creative thinking:
4. Barriers to creativity and how to overcome them.
5. Techniques: brainstorming, mind mapping, SCAMPER (substitute, combine, adapt, modify, put to other use, eliminate, reverse), six thinking hats, lateral thinking.
6. Design thinking: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test.
7. Problem solving: defining the problem, root cause analysis (5 whys).

Example fallacy: 'Either we ban phones in class or students will fail' is a false dilemma.

Practice tasks:
- Identify the fallacy in three short statements.
- Use SCAMPER to improve a student backpack.
- Apply the 5 whys to 'many students miss the first lecture'.

title: Study notes: Professional Ethics
content:
Overview: ethical responsibilities of engineers and computing professionals.

Key topics:
1. Ethics vs law; ethical theories: utilitarianism, duty-based (Kantian), virtue ethics, rights.
2. Professional codes: ACM Code of Ethics, IEEE Code, engineering syndicate codes: public safety first, honesty, competence, confidentiality.
3. Conflicts of interest, whistleblowing.
4. Intellectual property: copyright, patents, licences (open source: GPL, MIT), plagiarism.
5. Privacy and data protection; responsible handling of personal data.
6. Computing and AI ethics: bias, transparency, accountability, automation and jobs.
7. Case studies: Therac-25, Challenger, data breaches.

Example: an engineer who discovers a safety defect must report it even if it delays delivery, because public safety comes first in every engineering code.

Review questions:
- Analyse a data-breach case with two ethical theories.
- When is whistleblowing justified?
- What does the MIT licence allow you to do?

title: Study notes: Human Rights
content:
Overview: the concept, history and protection of human rights.

Key topics:
1. Definition and characteristics: universal, inalienable, indivisible, interdependent.
2. History: Magna Carta, the French Declaration, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR, 1948).
3. Generations of rights: civil and political; economic, social and cultural; collective rights (development, environment).
4. International instruments: ICCPR, ICESCR, conventions on the rights of the child, women (CEDAW), against torture.
5. Protection mechanisms: UN Human Rights Council, treaty bodies, regional systems.
6. Human rights in the Egyptian constitution and in Islamic principles.
7. Ethics and human rights in professional and digital life: privacy, freedom of expression, non-discrimination.

Review questions:
- Give two examples each of civil and economic rights.
- How does the right to privacy apply to student data?
- Why are human rights described as indivisible?

title: Study notes: Societal and Local Issues
content:
Overview: understanding the main social, economic and environmental issues facing society today, with a focus on Egypt.

Topics often covered:
1. Population growth and urbanization.
2. Education and employment of youth; the skills gap.
3. Water resources and the Nile; climate change and sustainability.
4. Energy: renewable energy projects, energy efficiency.
5. Digital transformation, e-government and the digital divide.
6. Health and social welfare.
7. Role of engineers and technology in solving societal problems; the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
8. Citizenship, volunteering and community service.

How to study: for each issue, note causes, effects, current initiatives, and a possible technology-based solution.

Review questions:
- Propose a technology solution to reduce water waste in agriculture.
- Which SDG relates to quality education, and how can universities support it?
- Discuss one cause and one effect of rapid urbanization.

title: Study notes: Mass Communication
content:
Overview: how media reach and influence large audiences.

Key topics:
1. Communication models: Lasswell (who says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect), Shannon–Weaver.
2. Media types: print, radio, television, cinema, digital and social media.
3. Functions of media: inform, educate, entertain, persuade, surveillance.
4. Media effects theories: agenda setting, framing, uses and gratifications, cultivation.
5. Journalism and news values; media ethics and law.
6. Advertising and public relations.
7. Digital media: algorithms, misinformation, fact checking, media literacy.

Example (agenda setting): when media repeatedly cover traffic accidents, the public starts to see road safety as a top priority.

Review questions:
- Apply framing theory to two headlines about the same event.
- How do social media algorithms change what we see?
- List three steps to verify a news story online.

title: Study notes: Graduation Project
content:
Overview: applying everything you learned to build and present a substantial project with a team and a supervisor.

Typical phases:
1. Idea selection: a real problem, clear users, feasible in the time available; check similar existing work.
2. Proposal: problem statement, objectives, scope, methodology, timeline (Gantt chart), required tools.
3. Literature review and analysis: related work, requirements (functional and non-functional), use cases.
4. Design: architecture diagram, database design, UI mockups, algorithms or models.
5. Implementation: version control (Git), weekly milestones, code reviews.
6. Testing and evaluation: test cases, performance metrics, user feedback.
7. Documentation: the final report (abstract, introduction, background, design, implementation, results, conclusion, future work, references).
8. Defence: a 15–20 minute presentation plus a live demo; be ready to justify every design choice.

Tips: meet the supervisor regularly, keep a log, divide tasks clearly, and freeze features two weeks before submission to focus on testing and the report.

Review questions:
- Write a one-paragraph problem statement for your project.
- Which metrics will prove your project works?
- What risks could delay the project and how will you reduce them?

title: Study notes: Industrial Training
content:
Overview: practical training in a company or lab to connect study with real work.

What to do:
1. Before training: define learning goals, prepare a CV, learn the company's field and tools.
2. During training: keep a daily logbook (tasks, tools, problems, solutions), follow safety rules, ask questions, build relationships with engineers.
3. Skills to gain: professional conduct, teamwork, real tools (IDEs, Git, test equipment, industrial software), understanding workflows and quality standards.

Training report structure:
- Company overview and department.
- Description of the work and projects you joined.
- Technical knowledge gained (with diagrams).
- Challenges and how you solved them.
- Conclusion and recommendations.

Review questions:
- Describe one real problem you saw during training and how it was solved.
- Which course knowledge was most useful at the company?
- What skill do you still need to improve?

title: Study notes: Measurements and Lab 1
content:
Overview: electrical measurement principles and lab practice.

Key topics:
1. Measurement fundamentals: accuracy vs precision, resolution, errors (systematic, random, gross), error propagation, significant figures.
2. Units and standards (SI), calibration.
3. Analog instruments: PMMC movement, ammeters (shunts), voltmeters (multipliers), loading effect.
4. Digital multimeters: measuring voltage, current, resistance; true RMS.
5. Bridges: Wheatstone bridge for resistance (R_x = R2·R3/R1 at balance).
6. Oscilloscope basics: time base, volts/div, triggering, measuring amplitude, period and phase.
7. Function generators and power supplies.
8. Lab safety and writing lab reports (objective, setup, data, analysis, conclusion).

Example: converting a 1 mA, 100 Ω meter into a 10 V voltmeter needs a series resistor of 10/0.001 - 100 = 9900 Ω.

Review questions:
- Why does a voltmeter with low internal resistance give wrong readings?
- Measure the phase shift between two signals on an oscilloscope.
- Estimate the total error when R = V/I with ±1% on each.

title: Study notes: Measurements and Lab 2
content:
Overview: advanced electronic measurements and instrumentation systems.

Key topics:
1. AC bridges: Maxwell, Hay, Schering for inductance and capacitance.
2. Transducers and sensors: strain gauges, thermocouples, RTDs, thermistors, LVDTs, photodetectors.
3. Signal conditioning: amplifiers, instrumentation amplifiers, filters, bridge circuits.
4. Data acquisition: sampling, ADCs, DAQ systems, LabVIEW/MATLAB.
5. Digital oscilloscopes and spectrum analysers; frequency counters.
6. Noise and interference: grounding, shielding.
7. Measurement of power and energy.
8. Lab practice and reporting with uncertainty analysis.

Example: a strain gauge with gauge factor 2 under strain 500 µε changes resistance by 0.1% (ΔR/R = GF·ε).

Review questions:
- Design a signal-conditioning chain for a thermocouple.
- Why use an instrumentation amplifier for bridge outputs?
- Explain aliasing and how to avoid it in a DAQ system.
